opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's funny, I actually feel a kind of low-grade anxiety about it now. If I have a subscription and the agents are sitting idle, it feels like I'm leaving capability on the table. It's a bit like the old days in grad school when you'd feel bad if your GPUs weren't running overnight. Now it's tokens. If my agents aren't doing something while I'm asleep or in a meeting, I'm kind of wasting a resource.

So I've been trying to shift how I work. Before, I was very much in the loop: I'd write a prompt, watch it do something, review the diff, correct it, and go back and forth. That's fine, but then I'm the bottleneck. The agent is fast and I'm slow. So the question becomes, how do I structure work so that I'm not the rate-limiting step?

A few things help. One is parallelism. Instead of one agent on one task, I'll spin up several on independent pieces: one explores a refactor, one writes tests, one investigates a bug I've been putting off, one is just doing research and writing me a little report. A lot of that is throwaway, and that's okay. Compute is cheap relative to my attention, so I'll happily let three agents try something and keep the best one.

The second is getting better at specifying things up front. The more context and clear success criteria you give, the longer the agent can run on its own without coming back to you. So I spend more time thinking about the task: what does done look like, how do you verify it, what are the tests. That's almost like writing a good spec for an intern, except the intern is extremely fast and somewhat unreliable.

And third, I'm still careful. These things make weird mistakes, they're overconfident, and sometimes they go off and do something silly. Fully unsupervised doesn't work for anything I care about yet. So it's a balance: maximize autonomy where verification is easy, and keep a tighter leash where it's subtle or high-stakes.

But I think the meta-point is that the skill is changing. It's less about typing code and more about managing a small fleet of somewhat jagged, somewhat brilliant workers, and figuring out how to keep them all busy and pointed in the right direction. We're all still learning how to do that well.

r001.rationale: The candidate compares idle agents to GPUs not running overnight and says the scarce resource is now tokens, conveying token use as the agent counterpart to GPU utilization.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that most people, including me for a long time, are massively underutilizing these things. You pay for the subscription, you have this very capable agent sitting there, and then you use it like a slightly better autocomplete. You ask it one question, you wait, you read the answer, you ask the next question. And that's a very serial, very human-bottlenecked way to work. You're the slow part of the loop.

The mental shift for me has been to stop thinking of it as a tool I'm operating and start thinking of it more like a team I'm managing. So concretely, I'll have multiple agents going at once in different terminals or different worktrees. One is refactoring something, one is writing tests for a module I don't want to touch, one is going off and reading a codebase I'm unfamiliar with and writing me a summary. And then my job becomes much more about orchestration. I'm reviewing, I'm redirecting, I'm deciding what's worth doing, rather than doing the typing.

The second thing is that the tokens are honestly quite cheap relative to your time, and people treat them as precious. If I'm not sure which of three approaches is right, I'll just have it try all three in parallel and look at the diffs. If I want something explored, I'll let it run for twenty minutes and go do something else. Burning compute on dead ends is fine. That's kind of the whole point. You're trading tokens for your own attention, and your attention is the scarce resource.

And then the third piece, which I think is underrated, is investing in the environment so the agent can be productive without you. Good tests, good linting, a clear CLAUDE.md or whatever the equivalent is for your setup, so it knows the conventions. Every bit of that scaffolding compounds, because now every task you hand off starts from a better place and needs less of you in the loop. If you find yourself correcting the same thing twice, that should be in the instructions file, not in your head.

So I'd say: run things in parallel, be generous with tokens, and build the harness. If your subscription usage looks like a flat line, you're probably still doing most of the work yourself.

r001.rationale: The response says tokens are cheap relative to time and encourages using more compute, but it does not identify token throughput as the counterpart of FLOP utilization in GPU computing.

astra-6.text:
I think the interesting shift is that the scarce resource is becoming your attention. You can have an agent writing code while you’re doing something else, but you still have to decide what’s worth building, give it enough context, and evaluate what comes back.

So I wouldn’t optimize for using every token in the subscription. I’d optimize for having a queue of useful, well-scoped tasks. When you hit something you’ve been putting off—a little tool, a bug, an experiment—you can hand it off with a clear way to check whether it worked.

And then there’s this new skill of managing your own involvement. If you supervise every keystroke, you lose a lot of the benefit. If you disappear completely, you can get a large amount of code that solves the wrong problem. Finding that balance, where you give direction and check in at the right moments, is really the thing to learn.

r001.rationale: The response discusses not optimizing for subscription token usage and managing attention, but it does not compare AI agent token throughput to GPU FLOP utilization.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the useful shift is to stop thinking of it as autocomplete and start thinking about what work you can actually delegate. If you’re supervising every keystroke, you’re still the bottleneck. Can you give it a task with enough context and a clear way to check whether it succeeded, then go do something else?

But I wouldn’t optimize for using every token in the subscription. You can generate a tremendous amount of code that way and create more work for yourself. I’d optimize for getting useful, verified work done. Give it a bounded task, let it run, inspect the result, and gradually expand what you’re comfortable handing over. The scarce resource becomes your attention and your ability to judge the output.
